title: Let the guest be a god
hookLine: a knock at the door just as dinner is served: the Upanishad says to make much food for exactly this
carry: let the guest be a god to you

cards: Dinner is on the table, exactly enough for the people sitting at it, counted out, served. And then a knock at the door.
A cousin passing through, a neighbor, a friend of a friend who's hungry and a little embarrassed about the timing. Everyone at the table does the same quick arithmetic.
The Taittiriya Upanishad, the same text where Bhrigu found food, has already thought about this knock, and its answer comes before the knock does. Today, food that doesn't stop at your own plate.

teach.b: Near the end of Bhrigu's story, the Upanishad gives this rule, paraphrased: do not turn away anyone who comes to your dwelling for shelter. And so, it says, gather much food, so there is food to give.
That's the answer to the knock. Not a quick calculation at the door, but a kitchen that cooks, from the start, for more than the people already sitting down.
Earlier, in its teaching to departing students, the same Upanishad says, in Sanskrit, atithi devo bhava: let the guest be a god to you.

teach.h: LET THE GUEST BE A GOD TO YOU
teach.b: The guest isn't a disruption to the meal; the guest is honored at it like a god. The Bhagavad Gita says it from the other side.

Krishna says, paraphrased, that good people who eat what remains after the offering are freed from their faults, but those who cook only for their own sake eat their own wrong. This lands in three places.
First, this is why a Hindu home feeds a visitor before asking anything else: the guest is honored as God arriving at the door. Food as practice is also food as hospitality.
Second, the order matters: offer first, eat what remains.
In some Hindu homes a first portion is set aside before the family eats, for a guest, for a cow, for the birds. Third, it's practical. Make a little more.
Keep a spare plate. The rule isn't a feeling about generosity; it's a way of cooking, decided before anyone knocks.

how: Hindu teaching treats feeding a guest as sacred, in the Upanishad's words, let the guest be a god to you; in some Hindu homes a first portion of the meal is set aside for a guest, a cow or birds before the family eats.

food that is fasted from, then shared out at a feast

s: the Taittiriya Upanishad says to cook just enough for your own household
it says turn no one away and gather much food, so there is food to give.
the Gita praises those who eat what remains after the offering
and says those who cook only for their own sake eat their own wrong.
in this teaching, the guest is a disruption to the meal
let the guest be a god to you: the guest is honored like a god at the table.

games.q: dinner is served, counted out for the family. someone knocks, hungry. what does the Taittiriya Upanishad say?
o: send them on to someone with more to spare.
turn no one away; that's why you make much food.
let them wait until the family has finished.
games.why: the Upanishad says not to turn away anyone who comes for shelter, and so to gather much food. the answer is decided in the kitchen, before the knock.

practice: Picture the place where you usually eat, add one more seat, and let a face come for it: a friend you haven't fed in a while, a neighbor, someone alone.
Hold that face kindly with the breath, or if no one comes, hold the empty seat itself, open. If you pray, hold that person in prayer.

wordCard.voice: Food as practice. In the Upanishad: turn no one away, and make much food; let the guest be a god to you. Food that doesn't stop at your own plate. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: atithi, guest. From the Taittiriya Upanishad's atithi devo bhava, let the guest be a god to you.

carryVoice: Your line: let the guest be a god to you. A kitchen that cooks for one more is ready for the knock. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 3.10 (do not turn away anyone who comes for shelter; therefore gather much food)
Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11 (the teacher's instruction to departing students: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be a god to you)
Bhagavad Gita 3.13 (the good who eat the remains of the offering are freed from faults; those who cook for their own sake eat sin)
